meta.title: Monolith to Cloud Migration
meta.summary: Move an on-premises e-commerce monolith and its Oracle database to the cloud one capability at a time with the strangler fig pattern: a router in front, new services behind it, change data capture between the databases, one writer per entity, and a rollback path at every step.

functional: Send each URL path to either the monolith or a new cloud service, and change that routing (paths and weights) without a deploy
Move capabilities one at a time: catalog first (done), orders next (in canary), then cart, checkout, customers and payments
Each new service owns its own database; it never reads or writes the monolith's tables directly
Keep the on-premises database and the cloud databases in sync with change data capture in both directions during the transition
Exactly one system writes each entity at any moment, so there are no dual-write conflicts
Roll a migrated path back to the monolith in minutes, without losing orders written by the new service
The monolith and the back office systems that read its database (fulfilment, returns, finance) keep working throughout
nonFunctional: No customer-visible downtime for any cutover; any write freeze for one entity lasts under 1 minute
Rollback of a migrated path (routing plus data ownership) completes in under 5 minutes
Change data capture applies changes to the other side within 5 s (p99), in both directions
Proxying a legacy path through the cloud adds no more than 10 ms at p99 compared with today
Losing one of the two hybrid connections causes no customer impact; the cloud side survives the loss of one availability zone
Traffic between the cloud and the data centre never crosses the public internet unencrypted

scale.label: Storefront traffic
scale.value: 4k requests / s average, 15k / s at sale peaks; about 70% are product and search pages, mostly served by the CDN

scale.label: Orders
scale.value: 150k / day, 60 / s at peak; 5% currently created by the new orders service

scale.label: On-premises database
scale.value: Oracle 19c, 9 TB, 1,400 tables, about 20 GB of redo per hour at peak

scale.label: Hybrid link
scale.value: 2 x 10 Gbps Direct Connect at two locations, 4 ms round trip, IPsec VPN as backup (about 1.25 Gbps per tunnel)

scale.label: Traffic over the link
scale.value: About 2k proxied requests / s and 1.5 Gbps at peak, plus about 2 MB / s of change data each way

scale.label: Programme
scale.value: 18 months: catalog migrated, orders in canary; cart, checkout, customers and payments still on-premises

slos.name: Storefront availability
slos.sli: Requests to shop.example.com that do not return 5xx, divided by all requests, measured at the router for migrated and proxied paths together

slos.name: Order placement latency
slos.sli: POST /api/orders responses under the threshold, divided by all of them, measured at the router whichever side served the request

slos.name: Proxy overhead on legacy paths
slos.sli: Legacy requests whose time at the router minus the on-premises load balancer's own time for the same request id is under the threshold, divided by all legacy requests (joined from both access logs)

slos.name: Copies stay current
slos.sli: Changes applied to the other database within the threshold of their source commit, divided by all changes, in each direction

slos.name: Copies agree
slos.sli: Rows that match between Oracle and the cloud database in the CDC task's row validation (it re-reads changed rows on both sides and compares them), divided by rows compared, per migrated entity

alerts.when: 5xx at the router burning the error budget 14.4 times too fast (checked over 5 minutes and 1 hour)
alerts.why: Shoppers cannot browse or buy, whichever side is failing.

alerts.when: 5xx at the router burning the error budget 2 times too fast over 6 hours and 3 days
alerts.why: A steady trickle of errors, often one legacy path or one link, that never pages but will use up the month's budget.

alerts.when: Orders service 5xx rate more than 1 point above the monolith's, or its p99 more than 300 ms above, for 5 minutes
alerts.why: The canary is hurting real orders. The alarm also switches the rule to forward only to the monolith automatically; a human must confirm the rollback finished and the reverse copy drained.

alerts.when: More than 1% of POST /api/orders slower than 800 ms for 10 minutes, and over 1 hour
alerts.why: Slow checkout loses sales. Usually the link (failed over to VPN) or a chatty new call to the monolith.

alerts.when: Apply lag above 60 s in either direction for 10 minutes
alerts.why: Fulfilment stops seeing new orders, and a rollback cannot hand ownership back until the reverse copy has drained, so the safety net is gone.

alerts.when: One Direct Connect connection or its BGP session down for 5 minutes
alerts.why: Traffic still flows on the other connection, but the next failure drops to the slow VPN backup. Restore redundancy in working hours.

alerts.when: Hourly reconciliation finds more than 10 mismatched rows for any entity
alerts.why: Silent drift between the copies, usually a type mapping or a skipped change. It must be fixed before the next cutover step relies on the copy.

alerts.when: More than 1% of legacy requests spend over 10 ms extra between the router and the on-premises load balancer, over 1 hour
alerts.why: The migration is making untouched pages slower: usually the link on its VPN backup, lost connection reuse, or one Direct Connect location carrying everything.

alerts.when: Oracle keeps fewer than 6 hours of archived redo beyond what capture has read, or the CDC user's password expires within 14 days
alerts.why: Either one breaks capture for good: past the archived logs, or with a locked user, the only way back is a full reload of the affected tables. Fix it the same day.

signals.name: Share of traffic served by the cloud
signals.why: The progress bar of the migration, and the first place a mistaken rule change shows up.

signals.name: Link utilisation and BGP state per connection
signals.why: Each connection must stay under 50% so either one can carry everything when the other fails.

signals.name: Apply lag by direction and table
signals.why: Forward lag delays the cloud copy; reverse lag delays the monolith and blocks a rollback.

signals.name: Canary against the monolith
signals.why: The rollback decision compares the two sides over the same minutes, not against a fixed number.

signals.name: Legacy calls per request
signals.why: Every call pays the link round trip. A rising count means a new service leans on the monolith instead of owning its data.

signals.name: Archived redo headroom
signals.why: If capture falls further behind than Oracle keeps archived logs, CDC cannot resume and the table needs a full reload.

signals.name: Orders per minute by side against last week
signals.why: The business check on the canary: the cloud side's share of successful orders should match its weight, and total orders should not dip when the weight changes.

debug.symptom: Pages still served by the monolith got slower after traffic moved behind the cloud router
steps: Compare request time at the router with request time on the on-premises load balancer: the difference is the link plus the router.
Check round trip time and utilisation on both Direct Connect connections; if one is down, traffic may be on the VPN backup, which adds latency and caps bandwidth.
Check connection reuse between the router and the on-premises load balancer: a new TLS handshake per request costs several round trips over the link.
Look for new chatty calls: an anti-corruption layer or migrated service calling the monolith many times per request, or monolith code calling a cloud service in a loop.

debug.symptom: Fulfilment cannot see some orders placed through the new orders service
steps: Check reverse apply lag and the CDC task's error table: a stopped task shows as growing lag, a rejected row shows as an apply error.
Look for constraint failures in Oracle, such as a column the new schema allows to be empty but the old one requires, or a status value the old check constraint does not know.
Check the loop filter: rows from the cloud must carry origin CLOUD so forward capture skips them, and the reverse task must not filter them by mistake.
Run row validation again for the affected hours on order ids starting with N- and replay the missing ones from the cloud database.

nodes.label: WAF
nodes.description: Web ACL attached to the CDN: managed rule sets, rate limits and bot rules for every path, migrated or legacy

nodes.label: Shoppers
nodes.description: Browsers and the mobile app calling shop.example.com

nodes.label: DNS
nodes.description: Points shop.example.com at the CDN. Moving this record once, at the start, put the cloud router in front of everything

nodes.label: CDN
nodes.description: Terminates TLS near shoppers, caches product pages and images, forwards everything else to the router

nodes.label: Strangler Router (L7)
nodes.description: Path, method and weighted rules decide per request: migrated paths go to cloud services, everything else to the monolith's on-premises IPs over the hybrid link

nodes.label: Catalog Service
nodes.description: Migrated first: products, prices and categories. Owns all catalog writes now

nodes.label: Orders Service
nodes.description: Being migrated: creates 5% of new orders (ids starting N-) and owns only those rows

nodes.label: Anti-corruption Layer
nodes.description: Translates between the new domain model and the monolith's internal SOAP API and codes, so legacy quirks stay out of new services

nodes.label: Hybrid Link
nodes.description: Private connection to the data centre: two dedicated connections at two locations, attached to the VPC through a transit gateway. BGP prefers the dedicated connections and moves to the site-to-site VPN only when both are down

nodes.label: Catalog DB
nodes.description: Source of truth for products since the catalog cutover; reverse CDC keeps Oracle's PRODUCTS table as a read-only copy for the monolith

nodes.label: Orders DB
nodes.description: Owns N- orders; holds a CDC copy of every monolith order so history is complete at the final cutover

nodes.label: CDC Replication
nodes.description: Full load, then change data capture: forward from Oracle redo logs into the cloud databases, reverse from the cloud databases back into Oracle, one writer per entity. On Google Cloud, Database Migration Service and Datastream only replicate into the cloud, so the reverse direction there needs a tool such as Oracle GoldenGate or Debezium. Row validation re-reads changed rows on both sides and compares them, which feeds the copies-agree check. The Oracle and database credentials it uses live in a secrets store with rotation

nodes.label: Monolith
nodes.description: The existing Java app tier behind an on-premises load balancer: cart, checkout, customers, payments, 95% of orders and the back office

nodes.label: Oracle DB
nodes.description: One large Oracle database shared by every module of the monolith, with supplemental logging on for CDC

flows.title: Place an order on the migrated path
flows.summary: A shopper in the 5% canary places an order. The orders service owns it, asks the monolith about customer and stock through the anti-corruption layer, and reverse CDC copies the order back to Oracle for the back office.

steps.label: resolve shop.example.com
steps.detail: The hostname moved to the CDN once, at the start of the migration, so every later step is a routing change in the cloud and never a DNS change that caches would delay.

steps.label: POST /api/orders
steps.detail: Order calls are never cached; the CDN terminates TLS close to the shopper and forwards the call to the origin.

steps.label: passed: POST /api/orders
steps.detail: The web ACL on the CDN checks every request against managed rule sets, rate limits and bot rules before it is forwarded, so legacy paths get the same protection as migrated ones without touching the monolith.

steps.label: forward to origin
steps.detail: The CDN has a single origin, so all decisions about which side serves a path live in one place: the router.

steps.label: rule: POST /api/orders weighted 5 / 95
steps.detail: Weighted target groups send 5% of new orders to the orders service and 95% to the monolith; stickiness keeps a shopper on one side for an hour so a checkout does not bounce between them.

steps.label: forward to orders service
steps.detail: This request drew the cloud side, so the new service will create and own the order. The router adds a trace id, which the orders service, the anti-corruption layer and a SOAP header to the monolith all carry, so one trace spans both sides of the migration.
steps.payload:
POST /api/orders HTTP/1.1
X-Amzn-Trace-Id: Root=1-6730c4a2-8d1e5b3f0a7c42e9b6d15f08
traceparent: 00-8d1e5b3f0a7c42e9b6d15f08c3a2e1d0-4f6a8b0c2d4e6f81-01
Idempotency-Key: 3b9e6d2a

steps.label: check customer, reserve stock
steps.detail: Customers and stock are still owned by the monolith, so the orders service asks the anti-corruption layer in its own terms instead of reading Oracle tables, which would tie it to the old schema forever.

steps.label: SOAP call over the private link
steps.detail: The layer translates the request into the monolith's internal SOAP API and sends it over the private connection, paying one 4 ms round trip.

steps.label: ReserveStock(CUST_NO, ITEM_NO, QTY)
steps.detail: The reservation is a write to stock, which the monolith still owns, so it happens in the monolith's own transaction and nowhere else.

steps.label: customer active, reservation r77310
steps.detail: The layer maps legacy codes such as CUST_STAT='A' and zero-padded numbers into the new model, so those quirks never leak into the new service.

steps.label: INSERT order N-8F3K2 owner=CLOUD
steps.detail: Orders created here get ids starting with N- and owner CLOUD, so every row has exactly one writer and the router can send later changes to the right side by id. The client's idempotency key is stored under a unique constraint, so a retried POST returns the existing order instead of creating a second one.
steps.payload:
INSERT INTO orders (order_id, customer_id, status, total_cents, reservation_id, idempotency_key, owner, origin)
VALUES ('N-8F3K2', 4471902, 'placed', 5998, 'r77310', '3b9e6d2a', 'CLOUD', 'CLOUD');

steps.label: read commit from the change log
steps.detail: Reverse CDC reads the commit from the cloud database's log, because fulfilment, returns and finance still read Oracle and must see the order within seconds.

steps.label: apply to Oracle over the link
steps.detail: Change data crosses the private link, not the internet, and is small: about 2 MB / s at peak.

steps.label: MERGE INTO ORDERS (ORIGIN='CLOUD')
steps.detail: The row keeps origin CLOUD, so forward capture skips it and the change does not loop back to the cloud.
steps.payload:
MERGE INTO ORDERS o USING (SELECT 'N-8F3K2' AS ORDER_ID FROM DUAL) s
  ON (o.ORDER_ID = s.ORDER_ID)
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT (ORDER_ID, CUST_NO, STATUS, TOTAL, OWNER, ORIGIN)
  VALUES ('N-8F3K2', '0004471902', 'P', 59.98, 'CLOUD', 'CLOUD');

flows.title: Add to cart on a legacy path
flows.summary: Cart is not migrated yet. No rule matches, so the router's default sends the request over the private link to the monolith, which works exactly as before.

steps.label: POST /cart/items
steps.detail: Shoppers use the same hostname for every page; they cannot tell which side serves which path.

steps.label: passed: POST /cart/items
steps.detail: The web ACL on the CDN checks every request against managed rule sets, rate limits and bot rules before it is forwarded, so legacy paths get the same protection as migrated ones without touching the monolith.

steps.label: forward to origin
steps.detail: Cart changes are per shopper and never cached, so the CDN passes them to the router.

steps.label: no migrated rule matches: default
steps.detail: The default action forwards to the monolith target group, whose targets are the private IPs of the on-premises load balancer, reachable only over the hybrid link.

steps.label: to 10.8.20.11:443 over the link
steps.detail: The request leaves the VPC through the transit gateway onto the dedicated connection, adding one 4 ms round trip; the router reuses connections so it does not pay a TLS handshake each time.

steps.label: POST /cart/items
steps.detail: The data centre firewall admits only the router's and the services' subnets, so the monolith is not exposed more widely than before.

steps.label: INSERT CART_ITEM, SELECT PRICE
steps.detail: The monolith reads the price from its PRODUCTS table, which is now a read-only copy fed by reverse CDC from the cloud catalog, so legacy code keeps working without knowing the catalog moved.
steps.payload:
SELECT PRICE, CURRENCY FROM PRODUCTS WHERE ITEM_NO = 1182;
INSERT INTO CART_ITEM (CART_ID, ITEM_NO, QTY, UNIT_PRICE) VALUES (77012, 1182, 2, 29.99);

flows.title: CDC keeps the cloud copy in sync
flows.summary: The monolith still creates 95% of orders and owns them. Change data capture reads Oracle's redo log and applies each committed change to the cloud copy within seconds, idempotently and in commit order.

steps.label: INSERT INTO ORDERS (owner MONOLITH)
steps.detail: The monolith owns this order, so only the monolith writes it; the cloud copy must follow for order history and for the final cutover.

steps.label: read redo since SCN 918273600
steps.detail: Capture reads Oracle's redo and archived logs instead of polling tables, so it sees every committed change in commit order and adds almost no load to hot tables.

steps.label: LogMiner / redo reader session
steps.detail: The capture user has only the log reading privileges it needs, and supplemental logging makes the redo carry full keys for every update.

steps.label: skip ORIGIN=CLOUD, map types
steps.detail: It drops rows that came from the cloud through reverse CDC to stop loops, and maps Oracle NUMBER, DATE and one-letter status codes to the cloud schema.

steps.label: UPSERT guarded by source SCN
steps.detail: Apply is an upsert that only moves a row forward in SCN order, so replaying a batch after a restart cannot overwrite newer data.
steps.payload:
INSERT INTO orders (order_id, customer_id, status, total_cents, owner, origin, src_scn)
VALUES ('48812209', 3390114, 'placed', 12050, 'MONOLITH', 'MONOLITH', 918273645)
ON CONFLICT (order_id) DO UPDATE SET status = EXCLUDED.status, total_cents = EXCLUDED.total_cents, src_scn = EXCLUDED.src_scn
WHERE orders.src_scn < EXCLUDED.src_scn;

steps.label: save last applied SCN
steps.detail: The checkpoint is saved after the apply commits; after a crash or a link outage capture resumes from here, as long as Oracle still has the archived logs.

flows.title: Canary misbehaves: orders go back to the monolith
flows.summary: The orders service starts failing. The router stops sending it new orders within seconds; the orders it already owns are drained to Oracle by reverse CDC before the monolith takes them over, so no order is lost or written by two systems.

steps.label: 5xx 4.1% vs monolith 0.3%
steps.detail: The canary is judged against the monolith over the same minutes, not against an absolute number, so a bad day for everyone does not trigger a rollback.

steps.label: rule: forward only to monolith
steps.detail: The alarm triggers a small function that replaces the weighted action with a plain forward to the monolith, so new orders go there within seconds with no deploy and no DNS change. Setting the canary's weight to 0 is not enough: with target group stickiness on, shoppers already pinned to the canary keep reaching it until their one-hour stickiness cookie expires.

steps.label: read remaining N- changes
steps.detail: Orders the canary already created are still owned by the cloud; before the monolith may change them, every one of them must be in Oracle.

steps.label: apply to Oracle
steps.detail: The drain goes over the same private link. The reverse stream carries only the canary's own writes, a few orders a second, so even minutes of backlog is a few thousand rows and clears in seconds.

steps.label: MERGE INTO ORDERS (ORIGIN='CLOUD')
steps.detail: Each change is applied in commit order, so Oracle ends with the same final state of every N- order as the cloud database.

steps.label: flip N- rows to OWNER and ORIGIN MONOLITH
steps.detail: Only when reverse lag is 0 does the rollback runbook, run as a monolith admin job, flip the canary's rows. Resetting ORIGIN as well matters: forward capture skips ORIGIN='CLOUD' rows, so without it the monolith's later changes to these orders would never reach the cloud copy. Forward CDC carries this update to the cloud database, which flips the owner there too.

steps.label: route /api/orders/N-* to monolith
steps.detail: Only after the ownership flip has committed does the rule for changes to N- orders point at the monolith, so there is never a moment with two writers.

steps.label: POST /api/orders
steps.detail: The next order from the same shopper is placed exactly as it was before the migration started.

steps.label: passed: POST /api/orders
steps.detail: The web ACL on the CDN checks every request against managed rule sets, rate limits and bot rules before it is forwarded, so legacy paths get the same protection as migrated ones without touching the monolith.

steps.label: forward to monolith
steps.detail: The monolith's order code was kept deployed and tested with synthetic orders during the canary, so the old path is warm and needs no redeploy.

steps.label: INSERT INTO ORDERS (owner MONOLITH)
steps.detail: Forward CDC keeps copying these orders to the cloud, so the canary can restart later from a complete copy.

notes.text: Strangler fig instead of a big-bang rewrite: every step is small, reversible and delivers value, and the monolith keeps the business running. The cost is a long period of running two systems: a router, a hybrid link, CDC in both directions and an anti-corruption layer that all go away at the end. Set a decommission date for each piece, or the in-between state becomes permanent.

One writer per entity, never dual writes. If a service wrote to both databases, a crash between the two writes, or two writes arriving in different orders, leaves copies that disagree with no way to tell which is right. Instead the owner writes only its own database and CDC copies from the owner's log. Ownership moves per entity (catalog), or per row with an owner column and an id prefix (orders during the canary), and every row has exactly one owner at a time.

If one dedicated connection fails, BGP moves traffic to the other within seconds when BFD is enabled on both ends (without it the default 90 s BGP hold timer applies), so each must run under 50%. If both fail, traffic falls back to the IPsec VPN at about 1.25 Gbps per tunnel, so one tunnel cannot carry the 1.5 Gbps peak: run several tunnels with ECMP on the transit gateway, or accept that legacy pages, cart and orders (which reserve stock in the monolith) slow down and time out at peak, since the router cannot shed load by itself. Migrated catalog pages keep working either way. If the VPN is lost too, legacy paths stop and CDC pauses, resuming from its checkpoint when the link returns, provided Oracle kept the archived logs, so retain at least 24 hours of them.

Latency, not bandwidth, is what the hybrid link punishes. One proxied page pays 4 ms once, but a page that makes 200 SQL calls across the link pays 800 ms, which is why the monolith stays next to its database and each new service moves together with its data. Keep calls through the anti-corruption layer coarse (one call per request, batch lookups) and cache stable reference data such as customer tier.

A dedicated connection is private but not encrypted: use MACsec on the 10 Gbps ports or run IPsec over it. Plan IP ranges so the VPC (10.64.0.0/16) does not overlap the data centre (10.8.0.0/14), allow only the router and service subnets through the data centre firewall, and give the CDC user only log reading rights on Oracle and write rights on the replicated tables. Card data stays with the on-premises payment module until payments migrate, which keeps the card data environment on-premises (any cloud component that still carries card data, such as the CDN, stays in scope, so confirm the boundary with your assessor).

Moving data from Oracle to PostgreSQL is a heterogeneous migration: convert the schema and stored procedures first (with a schema conversion tool, then by hand), run a full load of each table, then start CDC from the SCN the load was consistent at. Validate with row counts and checksums before any traffic depends on the copy, and keep reconciliation running until the Oracle tables are retired.

Putting the web ACL on the CDN, the one front door, protects the monolith as well as the new services, and the data centre's old perimeter firewall rules can be retired path by path. Run new managed rules in count mode first: legacy endpoints often send odd but valid input (SOAP-style bodies, long cookies) that a blocking rule would break. The router should accept traffic only from the CDN (a secret header the CDN adds, or the CDN's managed prefix list), or attackers can skip the WAF by calling the load balancer directly.

The router's rules are the migration's feature flags: which paths and what share go to the cloud live in the rule set, changed by a reviewed script or the alarm's function, never by hand in the console, and every change is logged so a bad routing change can be traced and undone. A config service or feature-flag tool is only needed once routing depends on who the shopper is rather than on the path.

questions.q: Walk through the 7 Rs. Which would you apply to the parts of this system, and why not refactor everything?
questions.a: Retire what discovery shows nobody uses, retain what cannot move yet (the payment module tied to a card terminal network), rehost (lift and shift to VMs) when a data centre exit date matters more than improvement, relocate (VMware Cloud on AWS or Google Cloud VMware Engine) to move whole VMware estates in weeks, repurchase where SaaS fits such as site search or email, replatform for small changes with managed gains such as Oracle to a managed database or the app onto containers, and refactor only where scaling or speed of change pays for it. Here catalog and orders are refactored because they change and scale the most, while back office modules may be rehosted or retired. Refactoring everything takes years and risk for modules whose only problem is where they run.

questions.q: Why catalog first and orders second? What do you leave until last?
questions.a: Start with a capability that has a clear seam, few writers and low risk: catalog is read-heavy, edited by a few merchandisers, easy to verify and benefits immediately from the CDN, and it proves the router, CDC and deploy pipeline. Orders come next because they have high value and their writes can be split by row, but they depend on customers and stock, hence the anti-corruption layer. Leave until last the modules that share transactions across many tables, such as checkout, payments and stock, and find seams by mapping which modules read and write which tables from database audit data rather than from the code's package structure.

questions.q: During the transition, why not have the orders service simply write each order to both its own database and Oracle?
questions.a: Two writes to two databases are not atomic: a crash between them, a timeout on one, or two concurrent updates applied in different orders leaves copies that disagree, and nothing tells you which one is right. The design keeps one writer per row (owner column and N- id prefix) and lets CDC copy from the owner's commit log, which preserves commit order and retries safely because applies are guarded by the source SCN. The price is replication lag of a few seconds, so reads that must see their own write go to the owner, and origin tags stop forward and reverse CDC from looping.

questions.q: Walk me through taking orders from 5% to 100% on the cloud with minimal downtime.
questions.a: Before any traffic, run a full load and forward CDC, reconcile counts and checksums, and shadow-read so the new service's answers match the monolith's. Then ramp new orders 5, 25, 50, 100% on canary metrics while the monolith still owns its existing orders. To finish, move ownership of the remaining monolith orders: briefly block updates to them (seconds, at a quiet hour), wait for forward lag to reach 0, flip their owner to CLOUD, point every order route at the new service and keep reverse CDC running so the monolith's back office and a rollback still work.

questions.q: A data bug in the new orders service is found two days after it reached 100%. Can you still roll back?
questions.a: Yes, as long as reverse CDC kept Oracle current and the monolith's order code stayed deployed: set the weights back, drain reverse lag to 0, flip ownership to MONOLITH, and fix the bad rows with a correction script run against whichever side is the owner. That is only possible if the new schema stayed reverse-mappable, so the rule is to make only additive schema changes until the old path is retired. The point of no return is when reverse CDC is switched off, so do that deliberately, weeks after 100%, and keep backups of both databases from the cutover.

questions.q: What does the hybrid link cost in latency and money, and how does that shape the design?
questions.a: Two dedicated 10 Gbps connections cost about 3,300 USD a month in port fees on AWS (similar on Google Cloud), plus cross-connect and carrier circuit fees, and data leaving the cloud over them is about 0.02 USD per GB against roughly 0.09 USD over the internet, with inbound free. Bandwidth is rarely the limit; the 4 ms round trip is, so services move together with their data, calls through the anti-corruption layer stay coarse, and the monolith stays next to Oracle. A site-to-site VPN is cheaper and quick to set up but slower and limited per tunnel, so it serves as the backup or as a stopgap while the dedicated circuits are ordered.
